domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The framework's core innovation is graph-based entity correlation and cross-document intelligence for discovering hidden compliance risks across financial systems, aligning with knowledge-base design. The talk addresses financial fraud detection, risk scoring, and regulatory compliance workflows across multiple jurisdictions. The framework was evaluated on 3M records across four jurisdictions and includes enterprise deployment considerations for production use. The talk involves multi-component architecture, probabilistic modeling, and cross-jurisdictional normalization requiring domain knowledge. This is a recorded conference presentation by an independent researcher on the AI Engineer channel. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct excerpts from the presentation.

summary: Varsha Shah introduces the fundamental compliance gap organizations face: while they generate vast amounts of financial data across payroll, tax, procurement, and transaction systems, existing rule-based and document-level NLP solutions validate each document independently, failing to detect sophisticated fraud patterns that only emerge when information is connected across multiple systems. Modern fraud exploits subtle cross-document inconsistencies rather than obvious errors within a single record. To address this, she proposes a framework with three complementary components. The first is a graph-based entity correlation engine that connects employees, vendors, accounts, transactions, and regulatory filings into a unified network. The second is an adaptive probabilistic risk model that combines multiple risk indicators such as anomaly strength, source reliability, and historic patterns to compute confidence-based risk scores, prioritizing cases that need immediate attention while reducing unnecessary investigations. The third is a cross-jurisdictional normalization layer that standardizes currencies, tax rules, reporting periods, and classification schemes so risks are evaluated consistently regardless of transaction origin. Evaluated on approximately 3 million financial records over five years across four regulatory jurisdictions, the framework achieved approximately 91% precision, 87% recall, and an F1 score of 0.89, with a 76% reduction in false positives and approximately 40% reduction in manual audit effort. The framework continuously improves through feedback: confirmed fraud cases strengthen future detection patterns, while false positives help refine risk scoring and reduce unnecessary alerts. This continuous learning cycle shifts compliance from reactive validation after issues occur toward predictive governance, where organizations ask what is likely to go wrong next rather than what went wrong. Successful enterprise deployment depends on four key considerations: seamless integration with existing ERP, payroll, procurement, and tax platforms; jurisdiction-specific configuration for local regulations; alignment with audit frameworks so investigators focus on prioritized risk cases; and scalability to process millions of records. The framework represents an important step toward enterprise financial governance where AI not only detects but anticipates and prevents risks.

sections.title: Introduction and Compliance Gap
sections.summary: Varsha Shah introduces herself and her research. She explains that organizations generate massive data across payroll, tax, procurement, and transaction systems, yet compliance teams struggle with hidden fraud because existing solutions analyze documents independently. The compliance gap is that critical risks only become visible when information is connected across multiple systems.

sections.title: Limitations of Traditional Document-Level Analysis
sections.summary: Traditional compliance systems validate each document against its own rules. Sophisticated fraud patterns do not appear within single documents but emerge only when multiple documents are analyzed together, revealing cross-document inconsistencies.

sections.title: Framework Overview: Three Components
sections.summary: The proposed framework has three complementary components: an entity correlation engine connecting related information across systems, an adaptive probabilistic risk model evaluating connected data using multiple risk signals, and a cross-jurisdictional normalization layer standardizing regulatory context across jurisdictions.

sections.title: Component 1: Graph-Based Entity Correlation Engine
sections.summary: The first component connects entities across payroll, tax, procurement, and financial systems into a unified network, identifying relationships between employees, vendors, accounts, transactions, and regulatory filings.

sections.title: Component 2: Adaptive Probabilistic Risk Model
sections.summary: The second component combines multiple risk indicators such as anomaly strength, source reliability, and historic patterns to calculate confidence-based risk scores. It prioritizes cases needing immediate attention, reduces unnecessary investigations, and learns from audit outcomes.

sections.title: Component 3: Cross-Jurisdictional Normalization Layer
sections.summary: The third component harmonizes financial data by standardizing currencies, tax rules, reporting periods, and classification schemes across jurisdictions, ensuring risks are evaluated consistently regardless of transaction origin.

sections.title: Evaluation Setup
sections.summary: The framework was evaluated using approximately 3 million financial records collected over 5 years across four regulatory jurisdictions, assessing performance under realistic enterprise conditions.

sections.title: Detection and Operational Results
sections.summary: The framework achieved approximately 91% precision, 87% recall, and an F1 score of 0.89. It delivered a 76% reduction in false positives and approximately 40% reduction in manual audit effort, consistently outperforming traditional rule-based approaches.

sections.title: Continuous Learning and Predictive Governance
sections.summary: The framework continuously improves through feedback: confirmed fraud cases strengthen future detection patterns, while false positives refine risk scoring. This creates a continuous learning cycle that shifts compliance from reactive issue identification toward proactive, predictive governance, enabling organizations to ask what is likely to go wrong next rather than what went wrong.

sections.title: Enterprise Deployment Considerations
sections.summary: Successful enterprise deployment depends on four key considerations: seamless integration with existing ERP, payroll, procurement, and tax platforms; jurisdiction-specific configuration for local regulations; alignment with audit frameworks so investigators focus on prioritized cases; and scalability to process millions of records, bridging the gap between research and practical adoption.

sections.title: Key Takeaways and Conclusion
sections.summary: Varsha concludes with four takeaways: significant compliance risks exist between documents, not within them; combining graph correlation, probabilistic risk modeling, and normalization creates a scalable approach; results demonstrate improved detection, reduced false positives, and lower manual audit effort; and continuous learning enables the shift from reactive compliance to predictive intelligence-driven risk management.
